Under elevated shear conditions, the immobilized aptamer undergoes mechanical unfolding, triggering TPA release. Optical tweezers-based single-molecule force measurements probing aptamer unfolding and refolding under constant force and varied relaxation periods revealed a narrow range of threshold forces (4-10 pN) governing the transition between folded and unfolded states. Under defined flow conditions in a microfluidic channel, single-molecule flow experiments demonstrated a flow-dependent TPA release profile, with the maximum mean release observed at 50 µL/min. COMSOL-based fluid dynamics simulations estimated a corresponding tether force of 4.76 pN and a shear rate of 3,512.9 s-1, consistent with pathological shear levels observed in stenotic vessels and aligning with optical tweezers predictions. The enzymatic activity of released TPA was confirmed by a clot dissolution assay, with the highest mean functional TPA-equivalent activity observed under the same flow condition. Together, these results demonstrate that TPA-SMORES enables mechanistically controlled, shear-triggered release of functional TPA, supporting its potential as a strategy for improving the spatial control of thrombolytic therapy.

articles.title: Time-resolved dual-channel fluorescent probe for the detection of hypochlorite and sulfites during ferroptosis.
articles.abstract: Ferroptosis is an iron-dependent, non-apoptotic form of programmed cell death closely associated with various diseases. It is characterized by intracellular lipid peroxidation (LPO) and glutathione depletion. The process of lipid peroxidation is regulated by reactive oxygen species (ROS) and reactive sulfur species (RSS). Detecting ROS and RSS species during ferroptosis is particularly crucial for related research. However, the continuous temporal monitoring of these substances during ferroptosis remains an area that has not received sufficient attention. In this study, we constructed fluorescent probes ISE and ISEO to detect HClO and HSO3- during ferroptosis. Probe ISE enables dual-channel detection of HClO and HSO3- in yellow and blue channels, respectively. Probe ISE exhibits response times of 3 s for HClO and 45 s for HSO3-, with detection limits of 23 nM and 7 nM, respectively. Probe ISEO detects HSO3- through a change in the yellow-to-blue ratio. Probe ISEO has a response time of 80 s for HSO3-, with a detection limit of 26 nM. Both the probe ISE and ISEO demonstrate excellent imaging performance for detecting exogenous and endogenous targets within cells. Furthermore, the robust performance of the probes ISE and ISEO during ferroptosis in cells and zebrafish makes them extremely valuable for ferroptosis research.

articles.title: Particle occupancy in mRNA lipid nanoparticles: Measurement, manufacturing determinants, and relevance to product quality.
articles.abstract: Encapsulation efficiency (EE) estimates the encapsulated fraction of measured RNA in an mRNA lipid nanoparticle (LNP) preparation, whereas particle occupancy measures the fraction of particles containing detectable RNA. Neither metric describes the full distribution of RNA among particles. Particle-resolved studies show that high bulk EE can coexist with RNA-negative particles and broad copy-number distributions, but reported empty-particle fractions vary with composition, preparation, and analytical method. This Minireview examines fluorescence spectroscopy, particle-resolved microscopy and RNA counting, mass spectrometry, and population-separation approaches, distinguishing direct RNA-sensitive measurements from inferred loading. It considers manufacturing determinants and evidence linking payload distributions to product performance. Process changes can alter loading without parallel changes in mean particle size. mRNA-expression, multi-cargo gene-editing, and adjacent siRNA-knockdown studies suggest possible functional consequences, although the independent effect of binary occupancy on potency remains unresolved. Historical lipid-mediated delivery experiments caution against assuming that eliminating RNA-negative particles always improves activity. Occupancy is therefore best considered a context-dependent extended-characterization metric for development and comparability. Product-specific evidence is needed to determine whether occupancy is a critical quality attribute. Its use in routine testing would also require a fit-for-purpose validated analytical procedure and an appropriate control strategy.

articles.title: Microneedle geometry modulates drug transport in transdermal delivery systems.
articles.abstract: Microneedles have emerged as a promising strategy for transdermal drug delivery, owing to their ability to bypass the stratum corneum in a minimally invasive manner and enable controlled drug administration. In practice, microneedles have been developed with a wide range of geometries to meet diverse requirements in delivery efficiency, targeting, and release kinetics. However, the role of microneedle geometry in governing delivery performance remains incompletely understood. In this study, a modelling framework is developed to systematically investigate the effects of microneedle geometry on drug transport across multilayered skin and into the systemic circulation. A set of quantitative metrics is employed to characterise both the magnitude and temporal dynamics of delivery, including peak concentration, time to peak, cumulative exposure, temporal dispersion, asymmetry, and residence time. To enable generalised comparison across different geometries, a geometric transport scaling index is introduced, which largely removes dependence on shape class and captures the overall influence of geometric variation. The results demonstrate that microneedle geometry exerts a strong and compartment-dependent effect on delivery behaviour, with distinct and often non-monotonic trends observed across the viable epidermis, papillary dermis, reticular dermis, and systemic circulation. Geometry-dependent trade-offs are identified between delivery efficiency, transport timescale, and temporal dispersion, reflecting competing transport mechanisms across skin layers and systemic circulation. In several cases, optimal geometric regimes are identified depending on the target compartment and therapeutic objective. Overall, this study provides mechanistic insight into microneedle-mediated drug delivery and establishes a quantitative framework for the rational design and optimisation of microneedle-based systems.

articles.title: A novel non-specific binding method enables measurement of the fraction unbound of beyond rule-of-five compounds.
articles.abstract: The accurate determination of the fraction unbound is critical for interpreting pharmacological and toxicological data and for predicting human pharmacokinetics, dose selection, and drug-drug interaction risk. Drug development is trending away from traditional rule-of-five physicochemical properties towards new chemical modalities which often have high lipophilicity. This presents the experimental scientist with additional challenges in measuring fraction unbound using traditional techniques such as dialysis systems by exacerbating practical limitations around non-specific binding, low recoveries, bioanalytical sensitivity, and poor diffusion across dialysis membranes. Whilst there is already a plethora of methods available to combat some of the challenges, based upon our experiences there is still a need to continue to add novel options to address the increasing chemical complexity of beyond rule-of-five compounds. Here, we describe a non-dialysis method that exploits the non-specific binding properties of compounds to determine fraction unbound over a broad dynamic range of concentrations. Through understanding the equilibrium between free compound in the incubation versus compound, which is non-specifically bound to labware, indirect determination of the free fraction within the matrix of interest can be calculated. The robustness of the fraction unbound measurement via this approach is increased by establishing a consistent fraction unbound value over a large range in incubation concentrations. A focused test set of compounds was used to evaluate the method and demonstrate that this approach could be used for compounds with significant non-specific binding which struggle to generate accurate data via many of the traditionally available techniques.

articles.title: Effects of Metformin and Omega-3 Fatty Acids on Neurobehavioural Outcomes in Letrozole-Induced Polycystic Ovary Syndrome Mice.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a common endocrine disorder associated with reproductive, metabolic, and neurobehavioural abnormalities, including anxiety, depression, and cognitive impairment. Omega-3 fatty acids have anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective properties that may ameliorate these complications. OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the effects of metformin, fish oil, and flaxseed oil on anxiety-like behaviour, depressive-like behaviour, locomotor activity, and cognitive function in a letrozole-induced PCOS mouse model. METHODS: Thirty female Swiss albino mice were divided into five groups: Control, PCOS, PCOS + Metformin, PCOS + Flaxseed Oil, and PCOS + Fish Oil. PCOS was induced with letrozole (2 mg/kg, orally). These neurobehavioral tests were conducted: Open Field Test, Elevated Plus Maze, Morris Water Maze, Forced Swim Test, and Actophotometer Test. Data were analysed using one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's post hoc test. RESULTS: The PCOS Group exhibited anxiety- and depression-like behaviours and impaired spatial learning and memory compared with controls. Treatment effects varied across behavioural domains. Fish oil improved selected behavioural outcomes, particularly immobility and locomotor activity, whereas effects on spatial memory and other measures were less consistent. Flaxseed oil and metformin showed moderate beneficial effects on the behaviour of PCOS mice. CONCLUSION: In letrozole-induced PCOS mice, metformin, flaxseed oil, and fish oil showed distinct impacts on neurobehavioral outcomes. The results indicate that several behavioural changes linked to experimental PCOS may be modulated by omega-3-rich oils; nevertheless, additional mechanistic and clinical research is required to determine their therapeutic significance.

articles.title: Estimation of respiration rate from nonclinical telemetry ECG data.
articles.abstract: Assays to assess respiratory function are included in the ICH S7A guidance for Safety Pharmacology, which identifies the core in vivo studies required to evaluate safety prior to First in Human (FIH) dosing. This requirement is most commonly met using dedicated stand-alone rodent respiratory studies that require additional studies and increased resources. More importantly, the demonstrated transitional value of dedicated respiratory endpoints to predict risk and improve FIH safety is lacking. As such, alternative approaches that utilize commonly collected signals from cardiovascular assessment studies, such as electrocardiograms (ECG), to calculate respiration rate (RespRate) as a biomarker of potential adverse effects are becoming increasingly relevant. In this study, we implement three algorithms developed to estimate ECG-derived RespRate (EDR) in humans on preclinical ECG data collected from dogs. We then compare EDR to the benchmark direct measure of RespRate derived from telemetry intra-thoracic pressure (ITP) sensors in 19 recordings. EDR obtained using the moment-based and principal component-based algorithms was not significantly different from the benchmark, based on a TOST (two one-sided tests) analysis with an equivalence margin of five breaths/min, in 100% and 89% of animals respectively. Furthermore, in a positive control study administering Theophylline, the PCA method detected a drug-induced increase in RespRate also present in the ITP data. Thus, EDR may provide a potential alternative to stand-alone respiratory assays, but further evaluation across a broader range of respiration changes, subjects, and ECG hardware is needed to establish the robustness of these algorithms.

articles.title: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) spheroid model exhibits a characteristic extracellular matrix-rich fibrous capsule hindering drug penetration.
articles.abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), or primary liver cancer, is one of the leading causes of mortality worldwide. Liver cirrhosis, characterized by deposition of excessive extracellular matrix (ECM) secreted by hepatic stellate cells (HSCs), is the major risk factor of HCC development. Although anti-fibrotic therapies hold great promise in the treatment of HCC, conventional non-animal models lack the complexity of the tumor microenvironment, especially its ECM component, driving efforts to develop more representative platforms. In this context, we bioengineered HCC spheroids by co-culturing human HCC cells (HepG2) with human HSCs (LX-2) in different ratios using a soft-embossed microwell array platform. HCC spheroids, depending on their exact composition, displayed typical HCC features, such as the presence of an ECM-rich capsule, as revealed by immunostaining of collagen type I on intact spheroids after tissue clearing. We hypothesized that the presence of this capsule, which is involved in several stages of tumor progression, could act as a 'protective barrier' that regulates the penetration and delivery of therapeutic agents. This hypothesis was confirmed using our bioengineered HCC spheroids, in which the combined presence of HSCs and ECM hinders the penetration and therapeutic efficacy of a model chemotherapeutics (doxorubicin). This could be improved by concomitant enzymatic degradation of the ECM-rich capsule. Altogether, we propose our HCC model as a relevant platform to study tumor-tumor microenvironment interactions, gain mechanistic insights into HCC, identify novel therapeutic targets and evaluate (combination) therapies targeting tumor-tumor microenvironment while integrating ECM degradation with the (targeted) delivery of therapeutic agents.

Case Report: Fatal varicella-zoster virus meningoencephalitis with Froin-like cerebrospinal fluid and hydrocephalus following pembrolizumab-containing chemoimmunotherapy.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: In patients receiving immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), central nervous system (CNS) infections may mimic or coexist with neurological immune-related adverse events (irAEs). ICI-driven immune dysregulation has been proposed to amplify inflammation against latent pathogens ("immunotherapy infections due to dysregulated immunity", ITI-DI), but this remains a hypothesis-generating framework rather than a validated diagnosis. CASE PRESENTATION: A 54-year-old man with stage IIIC lung adenocarcinoma developed a herpes zoster eruption and lumbosacral pain 7 days after the first infusion of pembrolizumab-containing chemoimmunotherapy, followed by rapidly progressive flaccid paraplegia, urinary incontinence, and declining consciousness. Intravenous acyclovir was not initiated until 20 days after rash onset. The first cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) sample was xanthochromic and coagulated spontaneously in the collection tube (Froin-like CSF), precluding protein measurement. A second lumbar puncture showed mild pleocytosis (8 cells/ μ  L; 70% neutrophils) and undetectable glucose; varicella-zoster virus (VZV) DNA was detected in CSF by post-mortem targeted polymerase chain reaction. Spinal Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed diffuse meningeal enhancement; follow-up cranial imaging showed acute hydrocephalus. Despite intravenous acyclovir, corticosteroids, and intravenous immunoglobulin, the patient died 43 days after pembrolizumab initiation. CONCLUSION: This case highlights VZV CNS infection as an important diagnostic consideration in ICI-treated patients who develop herpes zoster and neurological symptoms, because infection may mimic or coexist with a neurological irAE. The temporal relationship with pembrolizumab raises, but does not establish, the possibility that PD-1 blockade modified the inflammatory response. Prompt virological testing and adequately dosed antiviral therapy are central to management; the role of adjunctive immunomodulation remains uncertain and should be individualized.

articles.title: Machine Learning-Augmented Precision Dosing: Integrating Pharmacokinetic Modeling With Clinical Decision Support.
articles.abstract: Inter-individual variability in drug exposure can lead to ineffective therapy or toxicity, particularly in vulnerable patients. Routine model-informed precision dosing (MIPD) relies mainly on population pharmacokinetic (PopPK) models, Bayesian forecasting, and therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM). Physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) modeling has a complementary role in extrapolation to special populations, evaluation of drug-drug interactions, and simulation of unobserved scenarios, but it remains uncommon for bedside dose adjustment. Machine learning (ML) may provide additional support when critical illness, organ dysfunction, or polypharmacy creates complex nonlinear relationships. The increasing availability of electronic health records, real-world data, and high-dimensional biomedical datasets has accelerated interest in ML for precision dosing. ML can support exposure prediction, limited-sampling AUC estimation, outcome-risk stratification, and monitoring prioritization. Its clinical role depends on the decision target, the availability of concentration data, and whether pharmacological constraints are retained within the modeling architecture. This review covers direct prediction models, limited-sampling AUC estimators, hybrid pharmacometric-ML models, neural ordinary differential equation approaches, and reinforcement learning for sequential dose decisions. We examine data sources, feature engineering, validation, reporting, and governance across glycopeptides, beta-lactams, polymyxins, triazole antifungals, and immunosuppressants. We also describe a staged clinical workflow in which concentration measurements and mechanistic models are used to calibrate data-driven predictions, and we identify the evidence needed for clinical implementation.

articles.title: Pregnancy outcome after first-trimester exposure to JAK inhibitors - an evaluation of the German Embryotox cohort.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Janus kinase inhibitors (JAKi) are increasingly being used in the management of autoimmune diseases across rheumatology, gastroenterology, and dermatology, including in women of childbearing age. Consequently, pregnancies occurring during JAKi treatment are becoming more common. However, uncertainties regarding their safety during pregnancy remain, and current human data are insufficient to allow a comprehensive assessment of fetal risk. METHODS: Observational data of pregnancies with first trimester JAKi exposure, recorded in the German Embryotox database, was analyzed. Pregnancies were prospectively enrolled between January 1, 2017, and November 15, 2025. Study endpoints included major congenital anomalies, pregnancy loss, and neonatal parameters. RESULTS: The cohort comprised a total of 44 pregnancies exposed to baricitinib (n = 17), filgotinib (n = 3), tofacitinib (n = 8), or upadacitinib (n = 16). A total of 32 live births were recorded. Among these, two major congenital anomalies were observed, one ventricular septal defect and one hypospadias. Five spontaneous abortions occurred, including one case of fetal anencephaly, and seven elective terminations of pregnancy were reported. Additional neonatal assessments revealed two preterm births at 36 weeks' gestation, three infants born small for gestational age, and two newborns large for gestational age. CONCLUSIONS: The current evidence is insufficient to establish or exclude an association between JAK inhibitor exposure and adverse fetal outcomes. To date, the potential for harmful effects cannot be ruled out due to the limited available data. Therefore, routine use of JAKi during pregnancy is not recommended and treatment should be approached with caution, and requires a critical risk-benefit assessment until further data is obtained. TRIAL REGISTRATION: The study was retrospectively registered in the German Clinical Trials Register on March 16, 2026 (DRKS00039622).

articles.title: When drug repurposing backfires: antagonistic effects of ivermectin on cisplatin therapy in oral cancer.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Cisplatin (CIS) remains the gold standard chemotherapeutic agent for the management of oral cancer. However, its clinical efficacy is frequently limited by chemoresistance and dose-dependent toxicities. Ivermectin (IVM), a well-established antiparasitic agent with emerging anticancer properties, has been proposed as a potential adjuvant capable of enhancing the antitumor efficacy of CIS. METHODS: In vitro experiments were conducted on HN9 oral squamous cell carcinoma cells, while OEC normal epithelial cells served as control. The experimental evaluation comprised the MTT assay for cell viability, Annexin V/propidium iodide (PI) staining for apoptosis detection, cell cycle distribution analysis, quantitative real-time PCR (RT-qPCR) for the assessment of apoptotic, anti-apoptotic, and inflammatory gene expression, and oxidative stress assay. RESULTS: Contrary to expectations, the CIS-IVM combination demonstrated an antagonistic interaction in HN9 cells. This was evidenced by reduced cytotoxicity of the combination treatment compared to CIS monotherapy, as determined by the MTT assay. Additionally, the combination attenuated CIS-induced S-phase arrest and was associated with decreased expression of pro-apoptotic markers (BAX and Caspase-3). Differential modulation of TNF-α expression and glutathione levels further suggested complex interactions affecting inflammatory and oxidative stress pathways. These findings indicate that IVM may interfere with CIS-induced cytotoxicity, potentially through its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties. CONCLUSIONS: The present study demonstrated an unexpected antagonistic interaction between CIS and IVM in HN9 oral cancer cells. Further investigations are warranted to elucidate the underlying molecular mechanisms and to determine whether similar effects occur in other oral cancer models or in vivo settings.

articles.title: Activation of TLR4 promotes oxidative inflammation via NADPH oxidase signaling in platelets of subjects with autism spectrum disorder.
articles.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a complex neurobehavioral disorder where both immune system and neurological dysregulations are known to play crucial roles. Platelets are known to play key roles in systemic oxidative inflammation through production of oxidants. However, there is still scarcity of data regarding the role of blood platelets in ASD subjects. Platelets are known to express innate receptors such as toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4), transcription factors such as NFkB, and oxidative enzymes such as NADPH oxidase (NOX2), however the molecular mechanisms in generation of oxidative inflammation in platelets of ASD subjects have not been investigated until now. Therefore, this study was aimed at investigating expression of TLR4, NFkB, NOX2, reactive oxygen species (ROS) and lipid peroxides (a marker of oxidative damage on lipid membranes) in platelets of ASD children (n = 27) and typically developing children (TDC; n = 22) through molecular and biochemical analyses. Further, correlation analysis was carried out with severity of the disease. Our data showed an upregulated expression of TLR4 and p-NFkB in ASD platelets as compared to TDC platelets. Further, elevated TLR4/ NFkB signaling was linked with elevated NOX2-derived ROS and oxidative stress. It was confirmed by the utilization of NFkB and NOX2 inhibitors which caused reduction in LPS-induced ROS and oxidative stress in ASD platelets. Further, there was positive correlation between platelet oxidative stress and severity of the disease. Our data suggests that elevated TLR4/ NFkB signaling in platelets of ASD subjects might predispose them to increased systemic oxidative inflammation through NOX-2 derived ROS generation and oxidative stress.

articles.title: Physicochemical characterization of a bioactive Minthostachys verticillata nanoemulsion with enhanced antibacterial efficacy against veterinary pathogens.
articles.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance among livestock pathogens represents a growing challenge for veterinary medicine, underscoring the need for effective plant-based alternatives. This study describes the development and physicochemical characterization of an oil-in-water nanoemulsion incorporating Minthostachys verticillata essential oil (EO) and evaluates its biocompatibility and antibacterial efficacy. The EO, obtained by steam distillation (yield 4.8% v/w), was chemically characterized by GC-MS, revealing a pulegone-menthone chemotype. A series of nanoemulsion formulations were prepared by modulating surfactant composition and processing parameters, leading to the selection of an optimized formulation (NE2-S). This nanoemulsion exhibited a mean droplet size of 103.2 nm, low polydispersity (PDI = 0.279), and moderate electrostatic stabilization, complemented by steric stabilization provided by non-ionic surfactants (ζ-potential = -22.5 mV). Biocompatibility assessment using an MTT assay in murine fibroblasts demonstrated low cytotoxicity at concentrations up to 2500 μg/mL. Antibacterial evaluation against enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (ETEC) and Staphylococcus aureus revealed enhanced efficacy of NE2-S compared with EO, with two-fold reductions in both minimum inhibitory and bactericidal concentrations. Biofilm inhibition and eradication assays were additionally performed against the same field isolates. NE2-S showed a clear advantage over EO in inhibiting and eradicating ETEC F4+ biofilm, whereas its effect against S. aureus biofilm was more limited, with EO proving superior at eradicating pre-formed S. aureus biofilm. Overall, these findings establish a physicochemical framework linking nanoscale colloidal architecture to improved antibacterial performance, supporting the potential of this nanoemulsion platform as a promising antimicrobial strategy for the control of bacterial infections of veterinary relevance in livestock production.

articles.title: Mapping the Financial Risk of Iran's Pharmaceutical System: A Cross-sectoral Qualitative Study.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Financial risk in pharmaceutical systems extends beyond supply-chain interruptions and is shaped by macroeconomic, regulatory, and governance dynamics. In Iran, where the pharmaceutical sector is characterized by structural dependence on imports, fragmented governance, administered pricing, and persistent exposure to macro-financial volatility, evidence on how these risks are generated, transmitted, and managed across institutional domains remains limited. OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to provide a cross-sectoral mapping of key financial risks in Iran's pharmaceutical system and to examine the mechanisms through which these risks affect firms' stability and national medicine security. METHODS: An exploratory qualitative design was used, based on semi-structured interviews with 35 experts from regulatory and policy bodies, financial and insurance institutions, pharmaceutical manufacturers and distributors, academic institutions, and commercial stakeholders. Data were analyzed using thematic analysis. RESULTS: Thematic analysis identified four analytical dimensions-drivers, transmission channels, consequences, and control responses-across five interrelated financial-risk categories: liquidity risk, market risk, credit risk, political risk, and operational risk. Risks were described as mutually reinforcing through liquidity constraints, pricing instability, macro-financial volatility, informal credit allocation, implementation weaknesses, and sanctions-related pressures, thereby generating systemic effects across the pharmaceutical sector. The study contributes a novel cross-sectoral framework for understanding how macroeconomic, regulatory, financial, and governance-related risks interact to reinforce systemic financial instability in pharmaceutical systems. CONCLUSIONS: Financial risk in Iran's pharmaceutical sector is a system-level phenomenon arising from the interaction of macroeconomic instability, fragmented governance, and structural dependencies. Strengthening financial resilience will require integrated reforms in public financial management, pricing and credit governance, market-stabilization mechanisms, and depoliticized regulatory decision-making to safeguard both sectoral sustainability and national medicine security.

articles.title: Renal Dose-Adjustment Concordance in Critically Ill Patients with AKI and CKD: A Cross-sectional Study.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Kidney dysfunction complicates drug dosing in the intensive care unit (ICU). Guidance is well established for stable chronic kidney disease (CKD) but is less certain in acute kidney injury (AKI), in which renal function can change rapidly. OBJECTIVES: To assess concordance between prescribed maintenance regimens and reference-based renal dose-adjustment recommendations for adults with AKI, CKD, or AKI superimposed on CKD. METHODS: This cross-sectional study included 80 adults admitted to four ICUs in 2024. Acute kidney injury was classified according to the Risk, Injury, Failure, Loss, and end-stage renal disease (RIFLE) criteria using serial creatinine measurements and/or urine output, whereas CKD required documented chronicity. Cockcroft-Gault creatinine clearance (CrCl) was used to match patients to dosing-reference categories. Each patient-medication pair was classified once according to maintenance-dose amount and dosing interval, using UpToDate as the primary reference and the Sanford Guide as a supplementary source. RESULTS: Among 414 patient-medication pairs, 211 (51.0%; patient-level cluster-bootstrap 95% CI, 46.2%-55.8%) were discordant: 125 were lower and 86 were higher than recommended. Vancomycin (41.4%), ciprofloxacin (40.0%), and levofloxacin (40.0%) had the highest drug-specific discordance proportions. Nephrology and pulmonology had the highest patient-level service proportions (62.5% and 61.5%, respectively). CONCLUSIONS: Reference discordance was frequent, particularly for antimicrobials. Because measured exposure and clinical outcomes were unavailable, these findings identify regimens requiring review rather than confirming prescribing errors.

articles.title: Synthesis, characterization, and in vivo evaluation of desvenlafaxine decanoate, a new long-acting injectable antidepressant.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: The aim of this study was to design, synthesize, and characterize a novel long-acting injectable antidepressant prodrug, desvenlafaxine decanoate. SIGNIFICANCE: Long-acting injectable drugs represent a useful approach for the treatment of mental illnesses, since these formulations extend dosing intervals and are beneficial for patients unable to self-administer oral medication or to maintain adherence to treatment. Although some antipsychotic depot formulations are used in clinical practice, there is a lack of studies on long-acting injectable antidepressants. METHODS: This prodrug was synthesized by esterifying desvenlafaxine with decanoic acid, affording the target compound in 75% yield. Structural characterization was performed by 1H and 13C NMR, high-resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS), and high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC). An in vivo proof-of-concept study was conducted in mice following intramuscular administration of desvenlafaxine decanoate. RESULTS: A selective HPLC-DAD method was developed to separate desvenlafaxine succinate and desvenlafaxine decanoate, achieving retention times 6.08 and 15.70 min, respectively. LC-MS/MS analysis of plasma samples collected 2 hours after administration demonstrated significant levels of desvenlafaxine in systemic circulation. The plasma detection was a proof-of-concept for the in vivo hydrolysis of the ester prodrug. CONCLUSION: These findings support the feasibility of desvenlafaxine decanoate as a promising long-acting injectable antidepressant for patients requiring prolonged maintenance therapy.

articles.title: Correction: Applicability of NAMs to support a read-across based hazard assessment workflow for systemic toxicity: a conazole case study.
Decoding voltage-gated sodium channels structure: Molecular mechanisms linking architecture, function, and disease.
articles.abstract: Voltage-gated sodium (NaV) channels are critical transmembrane proteins responsible for the initiation and propagation of electrical signals in excitable tissues. They consist of a large α subunit and auxiliary β subunits. Together, the voltage sensing, ion selectivity, and rapid gating transitions regulate neuronal, muscular, and cardiac excitability. Recent cryo-electron microscopy breakthroughs have transformed the understanding of NaV structure-function relationships, revealing the asymmetric organization of voltage-sensing domains (VSD), the architecture of the DEKA selectivity filter, the mechanical coupling between S4-S5 linkers and S6 gating helices, and the allosteric mechanism by which the IFMT motif mediates fast inactivation. Across the nine human NaV isoforms, subtle structural divergences underlie distinct tissue distributions, biophysical properties, and disease susceptibilities, explaining the diverse channelopathies that range from epilepsy and cardiac arrhythmias to skeletal muscle disorders and painful neuropathies. These high-resolution structures also illuminate isoform-specific pharmacological pockets, including membrane-dependent cavities in VSD4 and dynamic fenestrations that govern state-dependent drug access, enabling the rational design of small molecules, peptide toxins, and hybrid therapeutics with improved selectivity. Advances in structural biology, biochemistry, and computation have established an integrated mechanistic model that connects NaV channel architecture to gating, inactivation, isoform-specific function, and human disease. This growing molecular atlas now supports next-generation precision therapies aimed at selectively modulating NaV channel activity in neurological, muscular, cardiac, and pain disorders.

articles.abstract: [This corrects the article DOI: 10.3389/fphar.2026.1897246.].
